items.prompt: Where can microbes live on or inside the human body?

options.label: On the skin, in the mouth, in the gut, and many other places
options.feedback: Correct. Microbes live on many surfaces and inside many parts of the body, including the skin, mouth, gut, nose, lungs, and more.

options.label: Only inside the digestive tract
options.feedback: Not quite. While the gut is a major home for microbes, they also live on the skin, in the mouth, in the nose, and in other areas.

options.label: Only on the outside of the body
options.feedback: Incorrect. Many microbes live inside the body, such as in the gut, mouth, and lungs, not just on the outside.

options.label: Only in places with visible dirt
options.feedback: That is a misunderstanding. Microbes live on clean skin and inside healthy body parts too, not only where dirt is visible.

items.ok_line: Microbes live in many parts of the body, inside and out.
items.ko_line: Microbes are found in many body sites, not just one or two.
items.exp_text: The human body hosts microbes at many sites, including the gastrointestinal tract, skin, mouth, nose, lungs, and even the surface of the eye. They are not limited to one organ or to the outside only.

items.prompt: Which types of organisms are included among human microbiota?

options.label: Only bacteria
options.feedback: That is too narrow. Besides bacteria, humans host archaea, fungi, protists, and viruses as well.

options.label: Only bacteria and viruses
options.feedback: Incomplete. Fungi, protists, and archaea also live on or in the human body, so the list is longer than just those two.

options.label: Bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists, and viruses
options.feedback: Correct. These five groups make up the human microbiota, along with the sites they live in.

options.label: Only microscopic animals
options.feedback: That is not right. Micro-animals can live on the body, but they are usually excluded from the definition of human microbiota.

items.ok_line: Humans host bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists, and viruses.
items.ko_line: The microbiota includes more kinds than just bacteria or viruses.
items.exp_text: The human microbiota includes bacteria, archaea, fungi, protists, and viruses. While micro-animals can live on the body, they are not usually counted as part of the microbiota.

items.prompt: What does the term 'commensal' mean for a microbe living on a human?

options.label: It causes disease whenever it is present
options.feedback: That is the opposite. Commensal microbes do not harm the host, so they do not cause disease under normal conditions.

options.label: It coexists without harming or benefiting the human
options.feedback: Correct. A commensal microbe simply lives alongside the human without causing harm or giving benefit.

options.label: It benefits the human while harming itself
options.feedback: That is not what commensal means. In a mutualistic relationship both parties benefit, but in commensalism the microbe neither helps nor harms.

options.label: It is always a virus
options.feedback: Commensal refers to the relationship, not the type of organism. Many bacteria and other microbes can be commensal.

items.ok_line: Commensal microbes live with us without helping or hurting.
items.ko_line: Commensalism means no harm and no benefit, unlike mutualism.
items.exp_text: Some microbes are commensal, meaning they coexist with the human body without harming or benefiting it. This is different from mutualism, where both the microbe and human benefit.

items.prompt: What is one example of a microbe harming a human through a metabolite it produces?

options.label: It produces extra oxygen
options.feedback: That is not correct. Oxygen is not a harmful metabolite mentioned; some microbes produce trimethylamine, which can be harmful.

options.label: It produces water
options.feedback: Water is not a harmful metabolite here. The example given is trimethylamine, which the body turns into a different compound that can cause harm.

options.label: It produces vitamins
options.feedback: Vitamins are generally helpful, not harmful. The harmful metabolite is trimethylamine, not a vitamin.

options.label: It produces trimethylamine
options.feedback: Correct. Some non-pathogenic microbes produce trimethylamine, which the human body converts into trimethylamine N-oxide, a substance that can harm the host.

items.ok_line: Trimethylamine from microbes can become harmful in the body.
items.ko_line: The harmful one is trimethylamine, not oxygen or water.
items.exp_text: Even microbes that do not cause disease can harm humans through the chemicals they produce. For example, some produce trimethylamine, which the body converts to trimethylamine N-oxide, a substance that can be harmful.

items.prompt: What does the term 'microbiota' refer to?

options.label: The collection of microorganisms living in a particular ecosystem
options.feedback: Correct. Microbiota refers to the total collection of organisms in an ecosystem, such as those on or in the human body.

options.label: The genes of all microorganisms
options.feedback: That is actually called the metagenome, not microbiota. Microbiota is about the organisms themselves, not just their genes.

options.label: Only the harmful microorganisms
options.feedback: No. Microbiota includes all microorganisms, whether harmless, helpful, or harmful, not just the harmful ones.

options.label: Only the viruses on the skin
options.feedback: That is too limited. Microbiota includes many types of microbes in many body sites, not just viruses on the skin.

items.ok_line: Microbiota is the whole set of microorganisms in an ecosystem.
items.ko_line: Microbiota is about organisms, not just genes or harmful ones.
items.exp_text: Microbiota refers to the total collection of organisms in a particular ecosystem, like the human body. It is a broader term than flora, which mistakenly suggests plants.

items.prompt: How many bacterial cells are estimated to be in the human body?

options.label: About 30 trillion
options.feedback: That is close to the number of human cells, not bacteria. The estimate for bacterial cells is around 38 trillion.

options.label: About 38 trillion
options.feedback: Correct. The human body is estimated to contain around 38 trillion bacterial cells.

options.label: About 2 million
options.feedback: That number refers to the estimated number of bacterial genes, not cells. The cell count is in trillions.

options.label: About 20,000
options.feedback: That is roughly the number of human genes, not bacterial cells. Bacterial cells number in the trillions.

items.ok_line: About 38 trillion bacteria live in the human body.
items.ko_line: The estimate is 38 trillion, not thousands or millions.
items.exp_text: The number of bacterial cells in the human body is estimated to be around 38 trillion. This is roughly the same order of magnitude as the number of human cells, which is 30 to 40 trillion.

items.prompt: How do the number of bacterial genes compare to the number of human genes?

options.label: They are about equal
options.feedback: That is not correct. Bacterial genes are estimated to be about 100 times more numerous than human genes.

options.label: They are about half as many
options.feedback: That is incorrect. There are far more bacterial genes, not fewer. They number about 2 million, while human genes are about 20,000.

options.label: They are about 100 times more numerous
options.feedback: Correct. The estimated 2 million bacterial genes are about 100 times the roughly 20,000 human genes.

options.label: They are about 10 times more numerous
options.feedback: Not quite. The ratio is about 100 to 1, not 10 to 1.

items.ok_line: Bacterial genes are about 100 times more than human genes.
items.ko_line: The correct comparison is 100 times more, not equal or fewer.
items.exp_text: The human body's bacteria carry about 2 million genes, while human cells have about 20,000 genes. That makes bacterial genes about 100 times more numerous.

items.prompt: What do the microbes that are expected to be present and normally do not cause disease get called?

options.label: Normal flora or normal microbiota
options.feedback: Correct. These are the microbes that are expected to be present and usually do not cause disease under normal circumstances.

options.label: Pathogens
options.feedback: That is the opposite. Pathogens are microbes that cause disease, whereas these do not under normal conditions.

options.label: Commensals only
options.feedback: Not entirely. While some are commensal, others have mutualistic relationships, so they are not all just commensal. The broader term is normal flora.

options.label: Mutualists only
options.feedback: That is too narrow. Some normal flora are commensal, some mutualistic, so the correct term covers both.

items.ok_line: Expected, harmless microbes are called normal flora.
items.ko_line: These are normal flora, not pathogens or only mutualists.
items.exp_text: Microbes that are expected to be present and normally do not cause disease are sometimes called normal flora or normal microbiota. This includes both commensal and mutualistic microbes.

items.prompt: Which body sites did the Human Microbiome Project focus on when sequencing microbial genomes?

options.label: Only the gut and lungs
options.feedback: Not correct. The HMP focused on skin, mouth, nose, digestive tract, and vagina, not just gut and lungs.

options.label: Only the mouth and skin
options.feedback: That is incomplete. It also included the nose, digestive tract, and vagina.

options.label: Only the digestive tract and vagina
options.feedback: Missing several sites. The HMP also focused on the skin, mouth, and nose.

options.label: Skin, mouth, nose, digestive tract, and vagina
options.feedback: Correct. These were the main sites the project focused on to understand the normal human microbiome.

items.ok_line: The project studied skin, mouth, nose, gut, and vagina.
items.ko_line: The HMP covered five body sites, not just one or two.
items.exp_text: The Human Microbiome Project sequenced the genomes of microbes living in the skin, mouth, nose, digestive tract, and vagina. These are the main sites where the normal microbiota was examined.

options.label: The human genome
options.feedback: No. The human metagenome refers to the collective genomes of the resident microorganisms, not the human's own genes.

options.label: The collective genomes of the resident microorganisms
options.feedback: Correct. In genomics, human metagenome means the combined genetic material of all the microbes living on or in the body.

options.label: The collection of all microbe species
options.feedback: That describes microbiota, not metagenome. Metagenome is about the genes, not the species list.

options.label: The DNA of a single bacterium
options.feedback: That is just one organism's genome. The metagenome includes genes from all resident microbes, not just one.

items.ok_line: Human metagenome is the combined genes of resident microbes.
items.ko_line: Metagenome is about microbial genes, not human genes or species.
items.exp_text: Human metagenome is another name for the collective genomes of all microorganisms that reside in or on the human body. It is the same as the term human microbiome when used in a genomic context.
